newsitem.title: ITALY: Hard-left leader warns of problems for Italy govt.
newsitem.headline: Hard-left leader warns of problems for Italy govt.

text.p: A leader of the hard-left party that gives Italy's ruling coalition its majority in parliament warned on Monday it might have to make "difficult decisions" soon over its support for Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government.

Armando Cossutta, president of Communist Refoundation, made his comments in an interview with newspaper Corriere della Sera a day after the close of a congress of the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS), the largest group in Prodi's coalition.

The congress, which re-elected Massimo D'Alema as party secretary, backed a document recommending an overhaul of "traditional" welfare policies, accentuating recent strains between the PDS and Communist Refoundation.

Cossutta, whose party has no ministers in the cabinet but secures Prodi his majority in the Chamber of Deputies (lower house), said the PDS congress had left the government "much weaker" because of what he perceived as a shift to the right.

During the congress D'Alema warned the small Marxist party that it could not hold the government hostage on social issues, otherwise the coalition would be forced to seek an accommodation with the opposition over reforms.
Cossuttta rejected D'Alema's warning as "blackmail" and said the party would continue to oppose cuts in pensions and health.

"In the next few weeks, we will have to make some very difficult decisions. After the PDS congress, the political framework has changed because of the internal rightward movement in the PDS," Cossutta said.
Opposition leader Silvio Berlusconi has hinted his block might help Prodi enact yet more tough budgetary medicine needed to help Italy qualify for the single European currency.

The government, which two months ago pushed an enormous 62.5 trillion lire ($37.7 billion) deficit cutting budget through parliament, is now working on a fresh package of measures to trim as much as 15 trillion lire off the deficit.
The small party Cossutta heads along with secretary Fausto Bertinotti refused to join the PDS in 1991 when the once-mighty Italian Communist Party (PCI) shed communism.
Cossutta criticised D'Alema's final address to the congress, in which the PDS leader called for the left and the right to work together to tackle key constitutional and welfare reforms.
"I'm saddened. the situation is very serious and it could lead to unpredictable and dangerous political repercussions," Cossutta told the newspaper.
Some members of D'Alema's own party accused him of cuddling up with the opposition.
The left wing of the PDS, about 18 percent of the party, did not approve of the welfare motion and did not vote for D'Alema.

The government, which took office in May, also came in for tough criticism at the congress from Sergio Cofferati, head of Italy's biggest trade union, CGIL, who attacked its employment policies and warned against cuts in the welfare state.
The criticism launched by Cofferati was particularly significant because the CGIL's policies have historically gone hand-in-hand with those of the Italian left.
In a highly public spat, D'Alema hit back at Cofferati, accusing his union of being "deaf and closed" and said it would be sidelined if it did not adapt to changing society.
